# Darīmukhajātaka (Ja 378)

**ID:** Ja 378
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Darīmukhajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Darīmukha the Priest’s Son
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja378
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Darīmukhajātaka* (Ja 378) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the Pali Tipiṭaka [SuttaCentral]. Its framing narrative is delivered by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana and concerns the Great Renunciation (*mahānekkhamma*), introducing the canonical verses that begin with *Paṅko ca kāmā* (“Pleasures of sense are but a morass and a mire”) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883; Narada 2008]. 

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as Prince Brahmadatta to the chief queen in Rājagaha, while on the very same day the royal family priest fathers a son named Darīmukha [Cowell 1897; Fausböll 1883, 1897]. The two grow up as intimate companions and travel to Takkasilā to master all the arts [Law 1926; Cowell 1897]. While wandering to Benares, omens reveal that the Bodhisatta will become king [Cowell 1897]. When the riderless royal festal car arrives at their park to select a successor for the deceased king of Benares, Darīmukha realizes the kingship is destined for his friend; rather than accepting life as an army commander or householder, he secretly slips away to take the ascetic life [Cowell 1897; Shaw 2014]. Darīmukha subsequently attains awakening as a *paccekabuddha* [Ray 1994; Fausböll 1883, 1897]. Later, residing at the Nandamūlakapabbhāra cave, Darīmukha travels through the air to visit his former companion in his royal pleasure park to urge him toward renunciation [Fausböll 1883; Narada 2008]. Reciting verses on the suffering of conception, birth, and the foulness and dangers of sensual desires (*kāma*), he exhorts the king to vigilance before departing like a golden goose through the sky [Shaw 2014; Narada 2008]. Persuaded by the discourse, the Bodhisatta renounces his kingship for the ascetic life (*isipabbajjā*), develops higher knowledges and meditative attainments (*abhiññā* and *samāpatti*), and attains rebirth in the Brahma realm [Fausböll 1883].

SuttaCentral notes four modern translations in four languages, with no curated external parallels recorded [SuttaCentral]. Automatically computed text-reuse data from DharmaNexus identifies nine internal Pali matches (1,094 characters) with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Tatiyo bhāgo), the longest match covering verses §2.4–4.4 of the text against commentary section §2143_4–2149, with no cross-language matches in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora [DharmaNexus]. Modern scholars cite the tale to illustrate ancient Magadhan education at Taxila [Law 1926], the nature of *paccekabuddha* insight and discourse [Ray 1994; Shaw 2014; Narada 2008], and early Buddhist literary examples of delusion and suffering caused by sensual craving (*kāma-taṇhā*) [Global Recovery 2010].

**Sources**

- [Ray 1994] Reginald A. Ray, Buddhist Saints in India: A Study in Buddhist Values and Orientations (1994) — Noted Darīmukha's awakening as a pratyekabuddha provoked by a falling leaf.
- [Narada 2008] Narada Mahathera, The Buddha and His Teachings (Revised 2008) — Quoted the Pacceka Buddha's verse address to the Bodhisatta on the morass of sense pleasures.
- [Global Recovery 2010] Symposium volume, Global Recovery: The Buddhist Perspective (2010) — Cited the jātaka as an example illustrating the perils of sensual craving.

- [Fausböll 1897] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 7: Index (1897) — Confirmed the identity of Darīmukha as the purohita's son in Rājagaha and paccekabuddha.

- [Shaw 2014] Sarah Shaw, The Spirit of Buddhist Meditation (2014) — Provided translations of the verses on the suffering of birth and conception and Darīmukha's departure.
